newsitem.title: UK: SFO welcomes court ruling, Sumitomo probe continue.
newsitem.headline: SFO welcomes court ruling, Sumitomo probe continue.

text.p: Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO) welcomed Thursday's judgment that it was not in contempt of court over the way it handled a raid in the Sumitomo Corp investigation, which it will now press on with.
"There was no contempt of court. The SFO always regarded the allegations as groundless, and we are glad the Divisional Court agrees," the SFO said in a news release.

Two senior judges ruled in the High Court that, although SFO director George Staple's staff had breached the spirit of court orders in a raid on an accountancy firm on December 6 last year, they were not in contempt.
The five SFO officials, Staple, lawyers Andrew Jackson and Christopher Walker, accountant Anne Dilks and computer expert Michael Hainey could, in theory, have been sentenced to prison.

"Members of the SFO carry out their duties in a proper and professional manner. Those involved in today's hearing are looking forward to getting back to work on the Sumitomo investigation," the SFO said.
The case followed raids by the SFO on the premises of Kay Accountants Ltd.

The SFO was accused of breaching a court order issued late on the day of the raid, banning them from milking information from six computers seized under search warrants, and ordering these to be returned to Kay.
The orders banning the SFO from downloading the machines and ordering their return were obtained by Kay director Jeffrey Green.

The SFO has the disputed material, which it will hand back, and then immediately ask for again under a Section Two notice of the Criminal Justice act of 1987 which compels the provision of information that is being sought.
The SFO, in liaison with investigators in Japan and the United States, is investigating the multi-billion dollar scandal that rocked world metal markets in June last year.
Japanese conglomerate Sumitomo fired its head copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka, alleging he was a rogue who admitted running up losses of $2.6 billion in unauthorised copper trading.
